services.title: Turn customer conversations into next steps.
services.intro: Give customers a helpful first response and your team a clearer next step. We build AI chat and voice agents that answer routine questions, gather order details, arrange bookings and follow up through your business tools. Requests that need a person go to your team.
services.outcome: Help customers get answers and move forward, while your team focuses on the work that needs a person.
audience: Businesses handling customer questions through chat and calls
Teams collecting details for new enquiries, orders and appointments
Sales and support teams keeping customer records and follow-ups in order
deliverables: Chat and call flows built around your customers
Approved answers, useful questions and clear routes to your team
Steps for collecting orders, making bookings and following up
Connections to the calendars, CRM and tools covered by your project
Tests with realistic examples and guidance for your team

process.title: Find the right starting point
process.text: We look at the questions customers ask and the tasks your team repeats. Then we choose a useful first process and define what it should do.

process.title: Build around your process
process.text: We prepare the answers, set up the required connections and define when the agent can act, ask for approval or pass a request to a person.

process.title: Test real situations
process.text: We try normal enquiries, missing details and unusual requests. Your team reviews the results before we agree on launch, monitoring and day-to-day use.

faq.q: Can this work with my website, phone, calendar or CRM?
faq.a: We first check the tools, accounts and access you have. Your proposal then lists the connections we can build, any setup required and the limits to plan around.

faq.q: Can an AI agent take orders or book appointments?
faq.a: Yes, where the required systems support it. The agent can collect details and carry out the actions you approve. An order or booking is confirmed only after the relevant system accepts it. Unclear requests can be passed to your team.

faq.q: How is an AI automation project priced?
faq.a: You receive a fixed quote for the agreed work, connections and team handover. Calling, messaging, AI usage, paid platforms and ongoing support are listed separately where they apply.

useCases.title: Customer questions, answered
useCases.text: Help customers find product and service information using answers you approve. Collect the details your team needs and offer a clear way to reach a person.

useCases.title: A clearer picture of each enquiry
useCases.text: Ask useful questions about what a customer needs. Summarise the enquiry and pass it to the right person with enough context to take the next step.

useCases.title: Order details, ready to act on
useCases.text: Collect product choices, quantities and delivery details. Let customers review their request, then pass it into your order process and report its status accurately.

useCases.title: A helpful first step on the phone
useCases.text: Handle routine inbound questions and requested callbacks with a voice agent. Capture why the customer is calling and arrange a transfer or team callback when needed.

useCases.title: Bookings with a clear confirmation
useCases.text: Collect appointment details, check the available times in your calendar and submit the booking. Confirm it once the calendar accepts it, and pass exceptions to your team.

useCases.title: Follow-ups with the details in place
useCases.text: Prepare or send the follow-ups you approve, update customer records and share conversation summaries. Set clear timing, review rules and stopping points for each process.

deliveryNotes.title: Your knowledge, useful answers
deliveryNotes.text: Choose the information the agent can use, who keeps it current and which questions need a person.

deliveryNotes.title: Important actions stay clear
deliveryNotes.text: Let customers review key order and booking details. Decide which actions need their confirmation or your team’s approval.

deliveryNotes.title: A clear route to your team
deliveryNotes.text: Introduce the AI assistant openly. Let customers ask for a person and pass along the conversation so they do not have to start again.

deliveryNotes.title: Control as your needs change
deliveryNotes.text: Set the rules for calls, callbacks and follow-ups. Decide who reviews exceptions and how your team can pause or adjust the process.

faq.a: The choice depends on your features, existing systems and editing needs. Our custom development work includes PHP, Laravel, React and Next.js. For a business site with everyday content editing, WordPress may also be a suitable option.

journal.title: A clear website brief starts with five questions
journal.excerpt: What should the site do, who is it for and what comes first? A few clear answers give your project a useful starting point.

sections.heading: 1. What should the website achieve?
paragraphs: Start with the job you need the website to do. Before choosing layouts or collecting design examples, write down the problem you want to solve and what a useful result would look like.
For example: “Help business owners understand our services and request a quote.” That gives your team a starting point for the pages, content and main call to action.

sections.heading: 2. Who will use it?
paragraphs: Describe your visitors and what they need. A new customer may want a simple explanation of your service. An existing customer may need support or order details. Include the questions people ask before they buy or contact you.

sections.heading: 3. What must the first version include?
paragraphs: List the essential pages and features, then put later ideas in a separate list. Explain features through a task: “Customers can send their project details and request a quote” gives the team something concrete to plan.

Describe what happens when that task is complete. Which details does the form collect? Who receives the enquiry? What does the visitor see next? These answers make the work easier to estimate and review.

sections.heading: 4. What do you already have?
paragraphs: Gather your logo, brand guidelines, useful text, product details and images. Add links to the current website and any tools it uses. If you share a design reference, say what you like about it: the menu, the spacing or the way a service is explained.

sections.heading: 5. Who decides, and what needs planning?
paragraphs: Name the people providing content, reviewing designs and approving the finished work. Include your budget range, target launch date and anything the project depends on. Your team can then turn the brief into a proposal with a clear scope, price and review process.
You do not need every answer on day one. Keep open questions visible and update the brief as decisions are made. A short, current document is more useful than a long one nobody works from.

journal.title: Should you improve your website or start again?
journal.excerpt: A confusing page, a broken form and an ageing platform need different solutions. Find the problem before choosing the size of the project.

sections.heading: Name what is getting in the way
paragraphs: If your website feels dated, first ask what is making it hard to use. Can customers understand your service, find a product and contact you? Can your team update the content without a struggle?
Write down each problem in plain language. This helps you decide which parts need attention and which still serve the business well.

sections.heading: Try the tasks that matter
paragraphs: Open the site on a phone and a larger screen. Find a service, read a product page, complete a form or work through an order. Note where you get stuck. Screenshots and a short list of steps give the team useful evidence to review.

sections.heading: See what a focused change could solve
paragraphs: When the structure and editing setup still fit your needs, a few improvements may be enough. Clearer service text, a simpler menu, a repaired form or a better product layout can each address a specific problem. Ask what needs to change and what should be checked afterward.

sections.heading: Know when a bigger change makes sense
paragraphs: A redesign becomes worth considering when the structure, visual style and main user journeys all need work. A rebuild may be needed if the current platform cannot support your requirements. Ask the team to connect each proposed change to a problem you have identified.

sections.heading: Compare the complete plans
paragraphs: Compare the cost, features, content work and time required for a focused update and a wider redesign. Include the practical details: product data, payment connections and the pages people already link to.
Plan for the work behind the pages too. Content may need moving, old links may need redirects and your team may need help learning a new editor. Those tasks belong in the proposal.

Choose the plan that fits your goals and the resources you can commit. Agree on the tasks visitors should be able to complete when the work is finished, and keep later ideas separate from the current project.

journal.title: Your first automation: start with one useful task
journal.excerpt: Choose a repeated task, define a useful result and give someone responsibility for checking it. Build confidence before adding more.

sections.heading: Choose a task you can explain
paragraphs: Look for work your team repeats in a similar way: collecting enquiry details, preparing a summary or drafting an answer from approved information. Choose a task with a clear starting point and a result someone can check.
Write down the steps. If they change every time, settle the process first. You will have a clearer idea of what to automate and where a person needs to decide.

sections.heading: Define what it can and cannot do
paragraphs: Decide what starts the process, which information it can use and what it should produce. Name the tools involved and the person responsible. Set approval rules for actions such as sending messages or changing customer records. A first version can simply prepare a draft.

For example, an enquiry process might collect the submitted details, flag anything missing and prepare an internal note. A team member can review the note and choose the next action. Describe that result before building.

sections.heading: Use AI where it has a clear role
paragraphs: A simple rule may be enough to place a completed form in the right list. AI can help summarise a message or prepare a draft reply. Give each step a clear purpose and decide how a person will review work that needs judgement.

sections.heading: Test the less obvious situations
paragraphs: Try missing details, unclear wording, duplicate enquiries and requests outside the process. Decide when the automation should pause and ask for help. Keep a record of what happened so the responsible person can find and correct a problem.

sections.heading: Check whether it helps your team
paragraphs: Look at the work the automation creates as well as the work it removes. How much checking does it need? Does the result help someone take the next step? Use your team’s examples to improve it.

Include tool costs, access permissions and ongoing maintenance in the plan. Once the first task works as intended, review whether another step is worth adding. Keep each new action clear so your team can stay in control.
